title: Modes of Convergence
intro: A sequence of random variables can converge in several inequivalent senses. Knowing which one a theorem gives you, and which implies which, avoids most of the confusion around the limit theorems.

items: Almost surely: $P\left(X_n\to X\right) = 1$. For almost every outcome, the sequence of numbers $X_n(\omega)$ converges.
In probability: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $P(\vert X_n - X\vert > \varepsilon)\to0$. Large deviations become rare, but need not stop.
In mean square ($L^2$): $E[(X_n - X)^2]\to0$. More generally $L^p$: $E\vert X_n - X\vert^p\to0$.
In distribution: $F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)$ at every point where $F_X$ is continuous. Only the distributions converge; the variables need not even live on the same space.

blocks.text: Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability, and so does $L^p$ convergence (by Markov's inequality); convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution. No other implications hold in general. Two counterexamples show it:

items: In probability but not almost surely: the typewriter sequence of indicators of intervals of length $2^{-k}$ sweeping across $[0, 1]$. Each $X_n$ is rarely 1, so $X_n\to0$ in probability, but every outcome is hit once per sweep, infinitely often.
In distribution but not in probability: $X\sim N(0, 1)$ and $X_n = -X$. Every $X_n$ has the same distribution as $X$, but $\vert X_n - X\vert = 2\vert X\vert$ never shrinks.

blocks.text: Two partial converses help: convergence in probability to a constant follows from convergence in distribution to it, and convergence in probability implies almost-sure convergence along a subsequence.

The tool for almost-sure statements. If $\sum P(A_n) < \infty$, then with probability 1 only finitely many $A_n$ occur. Conversely, if the $A_n$ are independent and $\sum P(A_n) = \infty$, infinitely many occur. Applied to $A_n = \{\vert X_n - X\vert > \varepsilon\}$: summable tail probabilities upgrade convergence in probability to almost sure, which is the usual route to strong laws.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
# The "typewriter" sequence: indicators of shrinking intervals that sweep [0,1] over and over.
# X_n -> 0 in probability (P(X_n = 1) = interval length -> 0) but X_n(w) = 1 infinitely often for every w.
def interval(n):
    k = int(np.floor(np.log2(n))); j = n - 2 ** k
    return j / 2 ** k, (j + 1) / 2 ** k
w = rng.random()
hits = [n for n in range(1, 2 ** 12) if interval(n)[0] <= w < interval(n)[1]]
print(f"for the outcome w = {w:.4f}, X_n(w) = 1 at n =", hits[:8], "... (once in every block of 2^k)")
print("P(X_n = 1) at n = 10, 100, 1000:", [round(interval(n)[1] - interval(n)[0], 4) for n in (10, 100, 1000)])
# Convergence in distribution without convergence in probability: X ~ N(0,1), X_n = -X for all n
x = rng.normal(size=10 ** 6)
print(f"X_n = -X has the same distribution as X, yet P(|X_n - X| > 1) = {np.mean(abs(2 * x) > 1):.3f} for every n")

blocks.text: Output of the run: for the outcome $\omega = 0.3663$, the typewriter sequence equals 1 at $n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 21, 43, 87, 174, \dots$, once in every block, while $P(X_n = 1)$ is 0.125, 0.016 and 0.002 at $n = 10$, 100 and 1000. For $X_n = -X$, $P(\vert X_n - X\vert > 1) = 0.617$ for every $n$.

blocks.title: A summable sequence
blocks.text: $X_n$ is 1 with probability $1/n^2$ and 0 otherwise. Does $X_n\to0$ almost surely?
solution: $\sum1/n^2 = \pi^2/6 < \infty$, so by Borel–Cantelli only finitely many $X_n$ equal 1, almost surely. Yes.

blocks.title: A non-summable independent sequence
blocks.text: $X_n$ are independent, each 1 with probability $1/n$. Does $X_n\to0$ in probability? Almost surely?
solution: Almost surely: $\sum1/n = \infty$ and the events are independent, so by the second Borel–Cantelli lemma $X_n = 1$ infinitely often. No.
blocks.answer: In probability yes; almost surely no

blocks.title: In mean square
blocks.text: $X_n = n\cdot\mathbf{1}\{U < 1/n^3\}$ with $U$ uniform. Does $X_n\to0$ in $L^2$? In $L^1$?
solution: $E\vert X_n\vert = n/n^3 = 1/n^2\to0$, so also in $L^1$ (as $L^2$ convergence implies).
